topic.name: Language Modeling
topic.description: Autoregressive sequence probability, contextual conditioning, and the limits of next-token objectives.

concepts.name: Autoregressive language modeling
concepts.description: Factoring a sequence probability into next-token conditionals over prior context while keeping learned parameters fixed at inference.

misconceptions.name: Parallel logits imply independent tokens
misconceptions.description: Mistakes parallel teacher-forced computation for a factorization that removes dependence on earlier tokens.
misconceptions.remediation: Write the sequence likelihood as a product of conditionals before reasoning about how those conditionals are computed.

misconceptions.name: Prompt conditioning retrains model weights
misconceptions.description: Treats an inference-time prompt as a parameter update rather than input context for a fixed model.
misconceptions.remediation: Separate changes to the conditional context from optimizer-driven changes to parameters.

misconceptions.name: Next-token likelihood certifies factuality
misconceptions.description: Equates probability under a text distribution with external truth or evidential support.
misconceptions.remediation: Distinguish modeling text continuation frequencies from verifying claims against the world.

questions.stem: A decoder is trained with teacher forcing, so logits for every position are computed in one parallel forward pass. Which statement correctly describes the modeled probability of the token sequence?

options.text: It remains a product of next-token probabilities conditioned on earlier tokens; parallel training does not remove that factorization.
options.rationale: Teacher forcing supplies every prefix at once, but each position still represents its conditional factor in the sequence likelihood.

options.text: It becomes a product of independent token marginals because positions whose logits are computed together no longer condition on prefixes.
options.rationale: Computational parallelism does not erase the causal context used by each position.

options.text: It is defined by prompt-specific weight updates because conditioning on earlier tokens retrains the decoder during each forward pass.
options.rationale: Conditioning changes activations and probabilities while the model parameters remain fixed during the forward pass.

options.text: It assigns factual confidence to the sequence because high teacher-forced likelihood verifies that each generated claim is externally supported.
options.rationale: Sequence likelihood describes fit to token patterns, not independent verification of factual claims.

questions.stem: Two prompts are sent to the same deployed language model with sampling disabled and no fine-tuning between requests. Why can the next-token distributions differ?

options.text: The model first predicts all tokens independently, then the prompt selects which marginal distribution should be exposed to the user.
options.rationale: Autoregressive predictions are conditional on context rather than selected from context-free token marginals.

options.text: The parameters stay fixed, while each prompt supplies a different prefix and therefore a different conditional next-token distribution.
options.rationale: Inference-time context changes hidden states and conditional probabilities without performing an optimizer update.

options.text: Each prompt performs a temporary training step on its own text, producing new weights that are discarded after the response.
options.rationale: Ordinary prompting is a forward-pass conditioning operation, not an implicit gradient update.

options.text: The prompt with the higher-probability continuation has supplied stronger evidence that the continuation's factual claims are correct.
options.rationale: Conditional probability under the model is not a factuality or source-support score.

questions.stem: An autoregressive model gives a fluent historical claim high continuation probability, but a trusted archive contradicts it. What conclusion follows from the language-model objective?

options.text: The contradiction occurs because the archive prompt silently retrained the model weights toward a different historical account.
options.rationale: Supplying or consulting context does not imply that the deployed model parameters were optimized again.

options.text: The claim should be accepted because a probable continuation under the text model carries stronger evidential status than an external record.
options.rationale: The objective learns token-distribution regularities and does not rank external sources by truth.

options.text: High continuation probability can reflect common textual patterns; factual acceptance still requires evidence outside the next-token likelihood.
options.rationale: Likelihood under a language model and warranted belief about the world are different quantities.

options.text: The archive and generated claim are independent token samples, so their disagreement does not reveal a limitation of conditional language modeling.
options.rationale: The generated claim is context-conditioned, and the disagreement directly exposes that text likelihood is not factual verification.

questions.stem: A deployed autoregressive model receives five worked examples in its prompt. Its parameter checksum is unchanged, yet its next-token predictions on a related query improve. Which explanation fits this observation?

options.text: The examples changed the conditional context processed by fixed parameters; they did not perform an optimizer update.
options.rationale: In-context examples alter the prefix and resulting activations while the deployed parameter values remain fixed.

options.text: The examples triggered a temporary gradient step, so the model used prompt-specific weights despite the unchanged checksum.
options.rationale: Ordinary prompting performs conditional inference, and an unchanged parameter checksum contradicts a weight update.

options.text: The model predicted context-free token marginals, then selected a better independent distribution after reading the examples.
options.rationale: Autoregressive logits are conditioned on the preceding context rather than chosen from independent token marginals.

options.text: The improved continuation score established that factual claims in the response gained external evidential support.
options.rationale: Improved conditional prediction does not independently verify claims against evidence about the world.

questions.stem: For a three-token sequence, a fixed autoregressive model assigns probabilities 0.50, 0.25, and 0.10 to each observed token conditioned on its preceding prefix. Which computation and interpretation are valid?

options.text: Multiply to obtain 0.0125, then interpret the factors as context-free marginals because their logits were computed in parallel.
options.rationale: The numerical product is right, but each factor is explicitly conditional on its prefix rather than a context-free marginal.

options.text: Multiply to obtain 0.0125, interpreting the result as the product of successive prefix-conditioned token probabilities.
options.rationale: The autoregressive chain rule assigns the sequence probability by multiplying the stated conditional factors.

options.text: Recompute the factors after a prompt-specific parameter update because conditioning each token retrains the model weights.
options.rationale: Prefix conditioning changes model inputs and activations without implying an optimizer step or new parameters.

options.text: Use the largest factor, 0.50, as the sequence's factual confidence because likelihood certifies external correctness.
options.rationale: Neither a token probability nor their product independently verifies the sequence's claims against external evidence.

questions.stem: A fixed autoregressive decoder uses teacher forcing on tokens x1, x2, x3 and computes all training logits in one parallel pass. What probability does the logit used to score x3 represent?

options.text: It represents p-theta(x3 given x1, x2), evaluated with the same fixed parameters as the other positions.
options.rationale: The third factor conditions on the observed prefix even when its logit is scheduled beside other positions.

options.text: It represents a context-free marginal p-theta(x3), because parallel logits remove dependence between token positions.
options.rationale: Parallel evaluation does not remove x1 and x2 from the conditioning context for the third factor.

options.text: It represents a probability under parameters retrained on x1 and x2 during that forward pass.
options.rationale: Teacher-forced conditioning changes inputs and activations, not parameters through an implicit optimizer step.

options.text: It represents the external truth probability of the claim containing x3, because likelihood scores factual support.
options.rationale: A token conditional under a text model is not an independent factual-verification probability.

provenance.source_scope: Brown et al. describes autoregressive language modeling and Murphy supports the probability chain rule. The three-token teacher-forcing presentation is original instructional synthesis.
provenance.independence_note: This intentionally reuses f_ar_teacher_forcing_factorization because it asks for one factor of the same prefix-conditioned product as the released teacher-forcing item; the scalar warm-up is dependent evidence.

questions.stem: Two training programs use the same fixed decoder and shifted examples. Program S evaluates prefix-conditioned token losses in a serial loop; program P evaluates the same conditionals in parallel. Ignoring arithmetic roundoff, what changes in the modeled sequence factorization?

options.text: Program P changes the factors into independent token marginals because simultaneous evaluation removes prefix conditioning.
options.rationale: The premise says P evaluates the same prefix-conditioned quantities; scheduling does not change their conditioning sets.

options.text: Neither schedule changes the product of prefix-conditioned factors; they differ in computation schedule rather than probability semantics.
options.rationale: Both programs evaluate the same conditional factors under the same decoder parameters.

options.text: Program S keeps fixed weights while program P retrains weights separately from each token prefix.
options.rationale: Parallel forward evaluation does not introduce token-specific optimizer updates.

options.text: Program P turns sequence likelihood into factual confidence because evaluating more positions together adds evidential support.
options.rationale: Scheduling token losses does not transform text likelihood into external verification.

provenance.source_scope: Brown et al. supports autoregressive conditional prediction and Murphy supports the factorization. Serial and parallel programs are stipulated to compute identical conditionals.
provenance.independence_note: This shares f_ar_teacher_forcing_factorization because it restates the same distinction between dependency semantics and parallel scheduling in a two-program audit.

questions.stem: During a teacher-forced forward pass with fixed parameters, the loss for target token xt is computed from its permitted prefix. A prefix input xk with k less than t is perturbed while later inputs remain hidden from position t. Which trace is consistent with autoregressive factorization?

options.text: The loss at t stays context-free because parallel token losses are independent marginals.
options.rationale: The loss at t is explicitly conditioned on permitted prefix inputs, including xk.

options.text: The perturbation performs a training update, so a weight change is required before the loss at t can change.
options.rationale: Changing a forward-pass input can change activations and logits with parameters fixed.

options.text: The loss at t may change through its prefix conditioning, while the decoder parameters remain unchanged.
options.rationale: Autoregressive dependence permits xk to affect the conditional at t without an optimizer step.

options.text: The loss change would certify that the perturbed prefix makes the target's factual claim more or less true.
options.rationale: A changed conditional loss is not a factuality judgment about the target content.

provenance.source_scope: Brown et al. supports prefix-conditioned autoregressive prediction and Murphy supports conditional dependence. The fixed-parameter prefix intervention is original synthesis.
provenance.independence_note: This remains f_ar_teacher_forcing_factorization because the intervention tests the same prefix dependence that defines the existing factorization family; counterfactual wording does not create independence.

questions.stem: A deployed model answers a query once without examples and once after three worked examples are prepended. The parameter checksum and optimizer-step count are unchanged, but the next-token distribution differs. Which explanation fits?

options.text: The examples select a context-free token marginal because autoregressive positions are independent at inference.
options.rationale: The next-token distribution is conditioned on the full supplied prefix rather than selected from independent marginals.

options.text: The examples performed an unrecorded parameter update even though both the checksum and optimizer count stayed fixed.
options.rationale: The observed controls directly support fixed-parameter conditioning rather than an optimizer update.

options.text: The changed distribution establishes that factual claims in the second response gained external evidence.
options.rationale: A distribution shift under a new prefix does not independently verify response claims.

options.text: The examples changed the conditioning prefix and resulting activations while the learned parameters stayed fixed.
options.rationale: In-context demonstrations can alter conditional predictions through input context without gradient-based learning.

provenance.source_scope: Brown et al. evaluates in-context demonstrations without gradient updates. The checksum and optimizer-count controls are stipulated diagnostic evidence.
provenance.independence_note: This intentionally reuses f_ar_fixed_weight_demonstrations because it repeats the same checksum-controlled inference as the released demonstrations item; the simpler contrast is dependent.

questions.stem: A prompt defines an unfamiliar label mapping with worked examples, then asks the fixed deployed model to label a new case. Removing the examples changes its output; no training API is called. What is the supported interpretation?

options.text: The examples condition the next-token distribution on the temporary label mapping while parameters remain fixed.
options.rationale: The mapping is conveyed through the prefix and affects inference-time activations.

options.text: The examples turn the label tokens into independent marginals selected after the rest of the prompt is ignored.
options.rationale: The output is conditioned on the worked examples and query rather than detached from them.

options.text: The examples fine-tune a prompt-specific parameter set even though no training operation occurs.
options.rationale: A forward prompt does not imply an optimizer-driven parameter update.

options.text: The examples make the selected label factually verified because higher conditional likelihood supplies external evidence.
options.rationale: Following an in-prompt mapping is not factual verification against the world.

provenance.source_scope: Brown et al. supports task conditioning through in-context demonstrations without parameter updates. The unfamiliar labels and removal control are stipulated.
provenance.independence_note: This shares f_ar_fixed_weight_demonstrations because the solution is the same fixed-weights-versus-example-conditioned-prefix distinction; changing the label task is not independent evidence.

questions.stem: Run P prepends demonstrations and performs a forward pass. Run F keeps the original prompt but executes an optimizer update on training examples before inference. Which audit distinguishes the two mechanisms most directly?

options.text: Run P makes token positions independent, while Run F preserves prefix-conditioned factors.
options.rationale: Both runs can use autoregressive prefix conditioning; the intervention differs in parameters versus context.

options.text: Run P changes context with the checkpoint fixed, while Run F changes checkpoint parameters through optimization.
options.rationale: Prompt demonstrations affect inputs, whereas the stated optimizer step modifies learned parameters.

options.text: Both runs retrain parameters because supplying demonstrations is itself a temporary optimization step.
options.rationale: Run P is explicitly a forward pass without an optimizer update.

options.text: The run with higher continuation probability has stronger factual evidence under either mechanism.
options.rationale: Conditional likelihood does not identify external evidential support.

provenance.source_scope: Brown et al. distinguishes in-context task conditioning from gradient-based parameter updates. The P/F controlled comparison is original synthesis.
provenance.independence_note: This stays in f_ar_fixed_weight_demonstrations because the keyed audit is the same fixed-checkpoint demonstration mechanism viewed against an explicit optimizer control.

questions.stem: A fixed autoregressive model assigns p(x1)=0.50 and p(x2 given x1)=0.40. Which sequence probability and interpretation are valid for x1, x2?

options.text: Use 0.20 but interpret both factors as context-free marginals because their logits may be evaluated together.
options.rationale: The number matches the product, but the second stated factor is conditional on x1.

options.text: Recompute 0.50 and 0.40 after a prompt-specific weight update because prefix conditioning retrains the model.
options.rationale: The fixed model evaluates the conditional factors without an optimizer step.

options.text: Use 0.20 as the product of the first-token probability and the second token's prefix-conditioned probability.
options.rationale: The two-token chain rule gives 0.50 times 0.40, which equals 0.20.

options.text: Use 0.50 as factual confidence for the sequence because the larger token likelihood certifies its claims.
options.rationale: A token factor is neither the sequence probability nor an external truth score.

provenance.source_scope: Murphy supports the probability chain rule and Brown et al. supports autoregressive language modeling. The two conditional values are original arithmetic synthesis.
provenance.independence_note: This intentionally reuses f_ar_conditional_likelihood_product because it performs the same multiplication of stated prefix-conditioned factors as the released three-token item.

questions.stem: Under one fixed model, sequence A has conditional factors 0.80 and 0.50, while sequence B has factors 0.60 and 0.60. Which likelihood comparison follows?

options.text: The comparison requires independent token marginals, leaving the supplied conditional factors unable to rank either sequence.
options.rationale: Autoregressive sequence probabilities are specifically products of conditional factors.

options.text: The model needs prompt-specific parameter updates before the two factor lists can be compared.
options.rationale: Both lists are already evaluated under the stated fixed model.

options.text: Sequence B is factually stronger because two similar factors provide more balanced external evidence.
options.rationale: Factor balance is not a factuality criterion, and likelihood is not external evidence.

options.text: Sequence A has likelihood 0.40 and sequence B has 0.36, so A has the higher model likelihood.
options.rationale: Multiplying each pair gives 0.80 times 0.50 equals 0.40 and 0.60 times 0.60 equals 0.36.

provenance.source_scope: Murphy supports multiplying conditional factors and Brown et al. supports autoregressive likelihood. The paired factors are original synthesis.
provenance.independence_note: This shares f_ar_conditional_likelihood_product because ranking the two sequences repeats the same product calculation twice; comparison does not create a new independent operation.

questions.stem: Three observed tokens have prefix-conditioned probabilities 0.50, 0.25, and 0.50 under a fixed model. Using natural logarithms, what is their summed negative log-likelihood?

options.text: It is log(16), because the conditional product is 0.0625 and negative log(0.0625) equals log(16).
options.rationale: Summing negative conditional log-probabilities equals the negative logarithm of their product.

options.text: It is the negative log of three independent marginals, because parallel evaluation removes their prefix conditioning.
options.rationale: The arithmetic may aggregate together, but each supplied probability remains prefix-conditioned.

options.text: It requires three prompt-specific optimizer updates before the log terms can be summed.
options.rationale: The factors are already specified under a fixed model and require no retraining.

options.text: It is log(16) units of factual error, because negative log-likelihood measures external falsehood.
options.rationale: Negative log-likelihood measures predictive fit to the token sequence, not factual error against the world.

provenance.source_scope: Murphy supports chain-rule products and log-likelihood aggregation; Brown et al. supplies the autoregressive setting. Numeric factors are original synthesis.
provenance.independence_note: This remains f_ar_conditional_likelihood_product because log aggregation is a monotone algebraic rewrite of the same stated conditional product and should not count independently.

questions.stem: A fixed language model assigns high probability to a common claim that a controlled measurement directly contradicts. What does the high model probability establish?

options.text: It establishes that parallel token predictions are independent of the prompt and measurement.
options.rationale: Autoregressive probabilities remain conditioned on their prefix; independence does not explain the conflict.

options.text: It establishes that the claim is probable under the model, while the measurement still governs external factual evaluation.
options.rationale: Model likelihood and evidence about the measured world are distinct quantities.

options.text: It establishes that evaluating the claim retrained the model parameters to favor that statement.
options.rationale: Scoring a sequence with a fixed model is inference, not parameter optimization.

options.text: It establishes that the claim is factually supported more strongly than the contradictory measurement.
options.rationale: Text probability does not override direct external evidence.

provenance.source_scope: Brown et al. supports next-token likelihood as a language-model quantity and Murphy distinguishes modeled probability from external measurement evidence. The controlled conflict is stipulated.
provenance.independence_note: This intentionally reuses f_ar_likelihood_factuality because it makes the same likelihood-versus-external-truth distinction as the released archive example.

questions.stem: A model's probability for sequence S is recorded under prompt P and fixed parameters. Later, a trusted experiment refutes S, but its result is not added to P and no parameter update occurs. Which quantities change from this event alone?

options.text: The experiment silently retrains the model, so its parameters and recorded probability change without new input.
options.rationale: External evidence outside the model call does not perform an optimizer update.

options.text: The recorded high probability remains proof of S, so the factual evaluation should ignore the experiment.
options.rationale: Model probability is not proof and cannot displace trusted contradictory evidence.

options.text: The recorded model probability under unchanged P and parameters stays fixed, while warranted factual assessment of S changes.
options.rationale: The model inputs and weights are unchanged, but the external evidence relevant to truth has changed.

options.text: The experiment has no bearing on S because parallel token probabilities make the sequence independent of external facts.
options.rationale: Token-factor dependence and external factual evaluation are different questions; the experiment directly bears on the latter.

provenance.source_scope: Brown et al. supports fixed-parameter conditional scoring and Murphy supports separating model probability from evidence. The experiment not entering the prompt is an explicit stipulation.
provenance.independence_note: This shares f_ar_likelihood_factuality because it counterfactually holds model context fixed while changing external evidence, the inverse presentation of the same likelihood-versus-truth boundary.

questions.stem: On held-out text, model A has lower next-token negative log-likelihood than model B. On a separately sourced claim-verification set, A has lower factual accuracy than B. Which report is justified?

options.text: A is factually superior because lower language-model loss certifies stronger external truth.
options.rationale: The separate factual evaluation directly contradicts treating predictive loss as a truth certificate.

options.text: The claim-verification prompts retrained A during evaluation, making its factual score incomparable with B.
options.rationale: Evaluation prompts do not imply optimizer updates, and none are stated.

options.text: The next-token comparison is invalid because parallel held-out logits measure independent token marginals.
options.rationale: Held-out autoregressive loss aggregates prefix-conditioned token probabilities even when computed in parallel.

options.text: A has better predictive likelihood and worse measured factual accuracy; report the two axes separately.
options.rationale: The two evaluations measure different properties and the observed rankings need not agree.

provenance.source_scope: Brown et al. supports next-token likelihood evaluation and Murphy supports probabilistic predictive metrics. The separate sourced factual benchmark and opposing rankings are stipulated.
provenance.independence_note: This remains f_ar_likelihood_factuality because the two-metric report operationalizes the same boundary between model text likelihood and externally verified factual correctness.

questions.stem: A fixed autoregressive model teacher-forces two sequences, [x1, x2, A] and [x1, x2, B], in the same parallel batch. Which factor comparison follows from their shared prefix?

options.text: The shared x1 and x2 prefix factors match; the final factor evaluates A versus B after that prefix.
options.rationale: The first two observed tokens and their conditioning contexts are identical; the continuation token differs.

options.text: Their factors are context-free marginals, so sharing x1 and x2 provides no conditional structure to compare.
options.rationale: Batch parallelism does not remove the prefix conditioning in either sequence.

options.text: Each sequence retrains a separate parameter set, so even its identical prefix factors need not match.
options.rationale: Teacher-forced batch evaluation uses the same fixed parameters for both examples.

options.text: Their matching prefix likelihood proves that claims expressed by x1 and x2 are externally true.
options.rationale: Agreement in model likelihood is not independent evidence about the world.

provenance.source_scope: Brown et al. supports autoregressive prefix conditioning and Murphy supports factorizing a joint distribution. The paired shared-prefix sequences are original synthesis.
provenance.independence_note: This intentionally reuses f_ar_teacher_forcing_factorization because comparing shared prefix factors applies the same conditional-product semantics as the released teacher-forcing item; batching two sequences does not create independence.

questions.stem: During teacher-forced training, the loss for target xt is evaluated using the observed earlier tokens from the training example rather than sampled earlier predictions. Which probability interpretation remains correct?

options.text: The target is scored as an independent marginal because the observed prefix is supplied in parallel.
options.rationale: The observed tokens are still the conditioning variables for the target factor.

options.text: The target is scored as p-theta(xt given the observed prefix), with theta shared across examples and positions.
options.rationale: Teacher forcing supplies the conditioning prefix but does not change the autoregressive factor being modeled.

options.text: The observed prefix performs a local optimizer update before xt is scored under new parameters.
options.rationale: Supplying training inputs to a forward computation is distinct from the later optimizer operation.

options.text: The target score measures whether xt states a fact supported by external evidence in the example.
options.rationale: A conditional token score does not perform factual verification.

provenance.source_scope: Brown et al. supplies the autoregressive training objective and Murphy supplies conditional factor semantics. The observed-prefix-versus-sampled-prefix contrast is instructional synthesis.
provenance.independence_note: This remains f_ar_teacher_forcing_factorization because identifying p(xt given x-before-t) is the same keyed operation as the existing family, expressed through the source of the training prefix.

questions.stem: A fixed deployed model first receives prefix P and then receives the extended prefix [P, z]. No training call occurs. Why may the next-token distribution after [P, z] differ from the one after P?

options.text: The distributions are independent marginals, and adding z selects a different context-free table.
options.rationale: The next-token distribution is conditioned on the supplied prefix rather than selected from a context-free table.

options.text: Token z performs a parameter update, so the extended prefix is evaluated by retrained weights.
options.rationale: The premise supplies no optimizer step; context can change activations with weights fixed.

options.text: The conditional context changed from P to [P, z], so fixed parameters may produce different logits.
options.rationale: Autoregressive inference maps each prefix to its own conditional next-token distribution.

options.text: Adding z supplies external factual evidence, so the new distribution becomes a truth probability.
options.rationale: A context extension does not convert model likelihood into factual verification.

provenance.source_scope: Brown et al. supports next-token conditioning on a prompt under fixed deployed parameters. P and its one-token extension are original synthesis.
provenance.independence_note: This intentionally reuses f_ar_prompt_conditioning because extending a prefix and comparing its next-token distribution repeats the same fixed-weights conditioning operation as the released two-prompt item.

questions.stem: Two different prompts occupy separate rows of one inference batch. They use one checkpoint, sampling is disabled, and there is no cross-example state. The rows produce different next-token logits. Which explanation is valid?

options.text: Batching makes the token logits independent marginals, and the row number selects which marginal appears.
options.rationale: Each row's logits remain conditioned on that row's prompt, not its batch index.

options.text: Each row performs a private training step, producing two temporary checkpoints inside the same batch.
options.rationale: The one-checkpoint premise and inference call provide no optimizer operation.

options.text: A row assigning a named continuation higher probability carries stronger factual evidence because likelihood scores truth across prompts.
options.rationale: A higher model probability for a continuation does not establish factual support for it.

options.text: One fixed checkpoint maps each row's different prefix to a different conditional distribution.
options.rationale: Shared parameters can produce different activations and logits from different input contexts.

provenance.source_scope: Brown et al. supports prompt-conditioned inference with shared model parameters. Separate batch rows and absent cross-example state are stipulated implementation conditions.
provenance.independence_note: This shares f_ar_prompt_conditioning because batch parallelism changes execution layout but not the same fixed-model, different-prefix conditional explanation.

questions.stem: An audit removes a policy paragraph from a prompt while holding the checkpoint, decoding settings, and remaining text fixed. The continuation logits change. What does this intervention directly support?

options.text: The removed paragraph was part of the conditioning context, so its ablation can change fixed-model predictions.
options.rationale: The controlled intervention changes prompt context while the stated parameter and decoding controls remain fixed.

options.text: The ablation changes which independent token marginal is exposed, rather than changing a prefix conditional.
options.rationale: Autoregressive logits depend on the whole permitted prefix and are not context-free marginals.

options.text: Deleting prompt text reverses a parameter update that the original paragraph performed during inference.
options.rationale: The fixed checkpoint rules out the claimed prompt-driven optimizer update.

options.text: The changed logits reveal which prompt version is factually true because likelihood measures policy validity.
options.rationale: A logit intervention does not evaluate either paragraph against an authoritative policy source.

provenance.source_scope: Brown et al. supports context-conditioned fixed-parameter inference. The paragraph ablation, fixed decoding settings, and observed logit change are stipulated controls.
provenance.independence_note: This remains f_ar_prompt_conditioning because it causally ablates part of a prompt but solves with the same context-change-versus-weight-change distinction; the intervention is dependent verification.

questions.stem: Request 1 includes worked demonstrations and produces an improved task response. Request 2 is a fresh stateless call to the same checkpoint with the demonstrations omitted, and its behavior returns to baseline. No training or optimizer step runs, and a checksum confirms that the weights remain unchanged across both requests. What mechanism fits the pattern?

options.text: The demonstrations create independent task-token marginals that persist outside the prompt.
options.rationale: The behavior follows prompt presence and does not demonstrate context-free or persistent marginals.

options.text: The demonstrations condition Request 1 through its prefix without a persistent parameter update.
options.rationale: The effect follows the examples in the request while the checksum and no-optimizer control rule out a weight update.

options.text: The demonstrations retrain the checkpoint, but the learned update disappears when a new request starts.
options.rationale: The explicit no-training control and unchanged weight checksum rule out a temporary or persistent parameter update.

options.text: The improved first response is more factually supported because demonstration-conditioned likelihood certifies truth.
options.rationale: Task behavior under examples does not supply external factual evidence.

provenance.source_scope: Brown et al. supports in-context learning without gradient updates. Fresh stateless request behavior and return to baseline are stipulated persistence controls.
provenance.independence_note: This intentionally reuses f_ar_fixed_weight_demonstrations because fresh-request loss of the effect tests the same transient context mechanism as the existing unchanged-checksum demonstration family.

questions.stem: Two prompts use the same worked inputs but swap the arbitrary output labels `mip` and `zog`. A fixed model tends to follow the mapping shown in each prompt. Which explanation is supported?

options.text: The label tokens are independent marginals, so their in-prompt mapping has no conditioning role.
options.rationale: The observed mapping-sensitive behavior shows that labels are interpreted within the prompt context.

options.text: Each swapped mapping fine-tunes new weights for `mip` and `zog` during the forward pass.
options.rationale: The premise fixes the model; changing examples changes context rather than parameters.

options.text: The worked examples alter the conditional context, allowing fixed weights to follow either temporary mapping.
options.rationale: The arbitrary mapping is specified in the prefix and can guide its continuation distribution.

options.text: The mapping followed with higher likelihood is the externally correct meaning of the arbitrary labels.
options.rationale: The labels are stipulated within each prompt, and likelihood does not establish an external true mapping.

provenance.source_scope: Brown et al. supports learning task behavior from in-context examples under fixed parameters. The arbitrary labels and mapping-swap intervention are original synthesis.
provenance.independence_note: This shares f_ar_fixed_weight_demonstrations because swapping an arbitrary demonstration mapping tests the same example-conditioned fixed-weight mechanism as other family members; the label names do not create independence.

questions.stem: A fixed model assigns prefix probability p(P)=0.20, with p(a given P)=0.50 and p(b given P)=0.25. For the one-token continuations Pa and Pb, which likelihood comparison follows?

options.text: The conditional factors are insufficient for comparison because parallel logits are treated as independent marginals.
options.rationale: The chain rule directly combines the shared prefix with each stated conditional factor.

options.text: The model needs a separate parameter update for a and b before their continuation probabilities can be compared.
options.rationale: Both conditionals are already defined under the same fixed parameters.

options.text: Pa is twice as factually true as Pb because its continuation likelihood is twice as large.
options.rationale: A model-likelihood ratio is not a truth ratio.

options.text: p(Pa)=0.10 and p(Pb)=0.05, so Pa has twice the model likelihood of Pb.
options.rationale: Multiplying the common 0.20 prefix factor by 0.50 and 0.25 gives the two joint probabilities.

provenance.source_scope: Murphy supports the chain rule and Brown et al. supplies the autoregressive context. The shared prefix and continuation probabilities are original arithmetic synthesis.
provenance.independence_note: This reuses f_ar_conditional_likelihood_product because the keyed comparison multiplies the same shared prefix factor into two conditionals; repeating the family calculation for a ratio is dependent.

questions.stem: For a fixed autoregressive model, p(x1)=0.30 and p(x1,x2)=0.12. Assuming p(x1) is positive, what conditional probability follows?

options.text: p(x2 given x1)=0.40, because 0.12 divided by the 0.30 prefix probability equals 0.40.
options.rationale: Rearranging p(x1,x2)=p(x1)p(x2 given x1) recovers the conditional factor.

options.text: p(x2 given x1)=0.12, because a parallel token score is an independent marginal equal to the joint.
options.rationale: The joint includes the prefix factor and must be divided by p(x1).

options.text: p(x2 given x1) requires retraining on x1 before a conditional can be recovered.
options.rationale: The two probabilities already determine the conditional under fixed parameters.

options.text: p(x2 given x1)=0.40 means the content of x2 is 40 percent factually supported.
options.rationale: A conditional token probability is not a factual-support percentage.

provenance.source_scope: Murphy supports recovering a conditional from joint and marginal probabilities; Brown et al. supplies the language-model context. Values are original synthesis.
provenance.independence_note: This shares f_ar_conditional_likelihood_product because division simply reverses the same chain-rule multiplication. Reverse wording and arithmetic do not establish independent evidence.

questions.stem: A sequence's prefix-conditioned token negative log-likelihoods sum to 2.0 under a fixed autoregressive model. Using natural logarithms, what sequence likelihood follows?

options.text: It is exp(-2), interpreted as a product of independent context-free token marginals.
options.rationale: The numeric inverse transform is compatible, but the token terms are stated as prefix-conditioned rather than independent marginals.

options.text: It is exp(-2), the product likelihood corresponding to the summed prefix-conditioned log losses.
options.rationale: If negative log likelihood is 2, exponentiating its negative recovers the conditional product.

options.text: It is unavailable until the sequence performs an optimizer update on its own prefix.
options.rationale: The aggregate loss already determines the fixed-model likelihood without retraining.

options.text: It is exp(-2) factual confidence, so the value directly measures external truth.
options.rationale: A sequence likelihood is a predictive text-model quantity, not factual confidence.

provenance.source_scope: Murphy supports log-likelihood aggregation and inversion; Brown et al. supplies the autoregressive model context. The total loss value is original synthesis.
provenance.independence_note: This remains f_ar_conditional_likelihood_product because exponentiating a summed log loss is algebraically equivalent to multiplying the same conditional factors and therefore dependent.

questions.stem: Nine of ten sampled continuations from one model repeat the same historical claim, but an authoritative archive contradicts it. What is the strongest supported conclusion?

options.text: The samples are independent token marginals, so their repeated claim has no relationship to model probability.
options.rationale: Repeated sampled sequences can reflect mass under the model's conditional distribution; they are not context-free token marginals.

options.text: Generating ten samples fine-tunes the model toward the repeated claim during the evaluation run.
options.rationale: Sampling from a fixed model is not an optimizer update.

options.text: The claim is common under this sampling setup, but repetition does not override the archive's factual evidence.
options.rationale: Model-consensus frequency and externally warranted truth are separate evaluations.

options.text: The nine-to-one sample majority certifies the claim as more factual than the archive record.
options.rationale: Repeated generation is not independent source verification.

provenance.source_scope: Brown et al. supports sampling from autoregressive language models and Murphy supports interpreting model probabilities. The sample count and archive conflict are stipulated.
provenance.independence_note: This intentionally reuses f_ar_likelihood_factuality because repeated sampling changes the observation of model preference but not the core likelihood-versus-external-evidence distinction.

questions.stem: Under one prompt, a fixed model gives a common but false technical statement higher continuation likelihood than a rare statement that a trusted reference verifies. Which interpretation follows?

options.text: The two continuations are independent token marginals, making their prompt-conditioned likelihood ranking invalid.
options.rationale: Autoregressive continuation likelihoods are valid conditional model quantities even when they disagree with truth.

options.text: Scoring the rare statement retrains the fixed model, so the two probabilities use different parameters.
options.rationale: Likelihood evaluation under the fixed model performs no optimizer update.

options.text: The common statement is better supported because higher continuation likelihood certifies external correctness.
options.rationale: The trusted reference provides the factual evidence, and the stated higher model likelihood does not overturn it.

options.text: The model prefers the common text, while external verification favors the rare statement.
options.rationale: Distributional typicality under a language model and warranted factual belief need not share an ordering.

provenance.source_scope: Brown et al. supports continuation likelihood under an autoregressive model and Murphy supports distinguishing modeled probability from evidence. The common-false and rare-verified contrast is stipulated.
provenance.independence_note: This shares f_ar_likelihood_factuality because reversing the likelihood and truth rankings directly exercises the same boundary as the existing archive and metric-axis items.
